idiom_name: Thread::Queue worker pool behind a hand-written IO.select loop (or the Fiber scheduler)
implementation_notes: Ruby supplies the primitives but not the architecture: Thread plus Thread::Queue are the queueing layer and the worker pool (producers push, N worker threads block in pop), while the asynchronous layer must be hand-written as an IO.select loop or delegated to the fiber scheduler that Fiber.set_scheduler installs. The GVL means this structure helps most for blocking I/O - which releases the GVL - rather than for CPU-bound work, so CPU-heavy stages need processes, not threads. Using a reactor framework such as async or EventMachine, or splitting the service, are the alternatives when the event loop must be robust.
code_sketch:
queue = Thread::Queue.new                                   # queueing layer
workers = Array.new(4) { Thread.new { loop { handle(queue.pop) } } }
loop do
  ready = IO.select([listener])                             # asynchronous layer
  socket = listener.accept_nonblock
  queue << socket                                           # hand-off
end
pitfalls: The GVL prevents parallel CPU execution, so a thread pool only overlaps I/O and blocking library calls; CPU-bound stages must fan out to processes.
Thread::Queue is unbounded and push never blocks, so an overloaded pool grows memory instead of applying back-pressure.
Exceptions raised inside a worker thread vanish unless the thread is joined or Thread.abort_on_exception is set, leaving silent worker death and a stalled queue.
